title: Online disinformation in the 2020 U.S. election: swing vs. safe states
screen_reason: Behavioural Twitter study (5.3M tweets collected 27 Oct - 3 Nov 2020; 3.3M after filtering) that classifies every shared link's publisher domain against NewsGuard and reports the percentage of shared URLs pointing to untrustworthy news publishers, separately for swing-state and safe-state tweets (Table 5). The denominator is links that were SHARED, so this is SHARING (content_share) under the §3 governing rule ('% of shared links unreliable is SHARING, not CONTENT').

estimates.country: U.S. (Arizona, Florida, Michigan, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Indiana, Washington, Louisiana)
estimates.measure_type: % of URLs shared in swing-state-associated 2020 US election tweets whose publisher domain is rated untrustworthy by NewsGuard
estimates.value_raw: 26.06 (Table 5, VALIDATED / Swing, column N; No. URL = 299,210)
estimates.denominator: 299,210 URLs shared in the 2,649,642 validated tweets associated with swing states (Arizona, Florida, Michigan, Pennsylvania); the denominator includes trustworthy (T), untrustworthy (N), platform (P) and NewsGuard-unclassified (UNC) links
estimates.definition: the link's second-level domain carries NewsGuard tag N ('untrustworthy news domain'); platform (P) and satire (S) domains are not counted as news
estimates.misinfo_def: "For evaluating the credibility level, the Newsguard metrics consider, e.g., whether the news source regularly publishes false news, does not distinguish between facts and opin- ions, does not correct a wrongly reported news."
estimates.source_quote: When looking at links pointing to untrustworthy news sites (N), the concentration for swing states - 26.06%. - is higher than
estimates.ground_truth_detail: NewsGuard publisher ratings, produced by expert journalists, applied at the second-level-domain level; tags T (trustworthy news), N (untrustworthy news), P (platform), S (satire), UNC (unrated). P and S domains are excluded from the news classification. No independent validation of the domain list is reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: In this study, our evaluation of untrustworthy content takes a distinct approach by cen- tering the attention on the source of the content, the publisher, rather than focusing solely on individual stories.
estimates.notes: Swing-state half of the paper's headline swing-vs-safe contrast; the safe-state row is the paired estimate. 'Validated dataset' = the entropy-based (BiCM + Louvain + label-propagation) filtering output, i.e. accounts in the main discursive communities. Keyword corpus = 16 candidate-x-state keyword pairs (Table 2), English-only, tweets naming more than one state dropped. The paper reports NO pooled swing+safe percentage, and computing one would be a forbidden cross-category sum, so no overall row exists. On the source_quote: the sentence continues '...for safe states - 22.25%.' but a running page header (Pratelli et al. EPJ Data Science (2024) 13:25, Page 16 of 23) is interpolated at that point in the extracted text, so the quote is truncated at the page break to stay verbatim.

estimates.page_loc: Sect. 4.4 and Table 5, p. 15-16; restated Sect. 5, p. 20
estimates.ground_truth_detail: NewsGuard publisher ratings, produced by expert journalists, applied at the second-level-domain level; tags T (trustworthy news), N (untrustworthy news), P (platform), S (satire), UNC (unrated). P and S domains are excluded from the news classification.
estimates.moderator_quote: We use a content-based approach to establish the association between each tweet and the state type (i.e., swing or safe). In practice, we first check each tweet - or retweet - for the presence of at least one state name from the selected list (e.g., Arizona, Florida, etc.). We then exclude any tweets that contain more than one state name
estimates.notes: Safe-state half of the paper's headline swing-vs-safe contrast. Note the safe-state sample is dominated by Washington (36,254 URLs of 34,586 validated) and New Jersey; Indiana and Louisiana contribute under 1,700 URLs between them in the raw data, so this estimate rests on a much thinner and less balanced base than the swing-state one.

missed_or_uncertain: Seen and deliberately NOT extracted: (1) Community x state-type breakdowns of the same measure (Table 5): REP swing N = 34.72%, REP safe N = 33.25%; REP-DEM-JOURN swing N = 2.59%, REP-DEM-JOURN safe N = 0.91%. These are subgroups by discursive community (effectively by party) and ARE a headline of the paper ('Most of the disinformation comes from the former'), so an adjudicator may legitimately want them as four extra SHARING rows; I kept only the two dataset-level rows under R4 (quality over quantity) and record the exact values here so nothing is lost. The 34.72 vs 2.59 gap is the single most striking number in the paper. (2) '93% of untrustworthy links (N) are shared within the two main political communities. In particular, about 91% of the total is shared within the Rep community.' — reads as concentration, but the paper never states the Rep community as a PERCENTAGE of users (269,019 of 701,828 would be my own computation), so R1's requirement for both conc_group_pct and conc_share_pct is unmet and no CONCENTRATION row is possible. (3) Bot composition inside the misinformation set: 'of the 91% of the total in swing states, more than 74% are posted or retweeted by bots' (Table 9: 74.15% swing, 68.75% safe, VALIDATED, N links) — this is authorship inside a misinformation-only set, not a prevalence share, and bot/human status is not a veracity judgement, so it is not an eligible construct. (4) 'Tweets associated with swing states account for about 88% of the whole traffic' — volume of election talk, not misinformation. (5) Trustworthy-link shares (T: 28.30% swing, 50.66% safe) — the complement class, not misinformation. (6) Average sharing intensity of untrustworthy links (57 shares per N link in Rep vs 7 in Rep-Dem-Journ; 66 swing vs 22 safe) — a per-link virality mean, not a share of anything, and its denominator is the misinformation set itself. (7) Table 9's classified-account subset (78,439 all links, 20,627 N links) would yield 26.3%, but that base is only the first and last bot-score deciles, a non-representative subpopulation, so I did not use it. NOTE that the paper's own abstract/results text rounds the swing-state figure differently in places ('26.06%.' with a stray period); the Table 5 value is authoritative.

rob.design: Streaming Twitter API collection of ~5.3M tweets, 27 Oct - 3 Nov 2020, driven by 16 keyword pairs combining each of 8 states (4 swing, 4 safe, chosen from Cook Political Report ratings) with 'biden'/'trump'. Tweets naming more than one state dropped (~1.5M) and non-English dropped (~422k), leaving ~3.3M tweets and ~398k URLs. Link publishers classified by NewsGuard domain ratings (expert journalist annotation), not by story-level fact-checking. Users classified as bot/non-bot with BotometerLite v4, keeping only the first and last bot-score deciles ([0, 0.04] and [0.45, 1]). Discursive communities derived by Bipartite Configuration Model validation of the verified-unverified retweet network, Louvain community detection, then label propagation; validation of the community labels against manual annotation of 99 randomly selected unverified accounts gave 89/99 consistent. No survey, no response rate; no intercoder-reliability statistic for the NewsGuard ratings themselves. Author-stated limitations: only 8 of 50 states, only the 2020 election, one week, dataset not rehydratable after the Twitter API change.
